questions.prompt: Gradients for two tensors have norms 6 and 8. With global-norm clipping at max_norm = 5, what are their norms afterwards?
questions.explanation: The global norm is √(36 + 64) = 10, so every tensor is scaled by 5/10. That gives 3 and 4, and the direction is preserved. Per-tensor clipping would give 5 and 5, which changes the direction.

questions.prompt: During BPTT for a vanilla RNN, what is the total gradient reaching h_t?
options: Only the loss gradient at step t
Only the gradient flowing back from h_{t+1}
The loss gradient at step t plus the gradient flowing back from h_{t+1}
The average of the gradients over all steps
questions.explanation: h_t affects the loss directly (if read at step t) and indirectly through every later step via h_{t+1}. Both contributions add.

questions.prompt: In an LSTM, which of i, f, g, o uses tanh instead of a sigmoid?
questions.explanation: i, f and o are gates, scaling factors in (0, 1). g is the content written to the cell, so it needs both signs and uses tanh, with range (−1, 1).

questions.prompt: Why can an LSTM carry information across many more steps than a vanilla RNN?
options: Its cell state is updated additively, so with f ≈ 1 it (and its gradient) passes through nearly unchanged
It uses ReLU instead of tanh
It processes the sequence in both directions
questions.explanation: c_t = f ⊙ c_{t−1} + i ⊙ g. When the forget gate stays near 1, the cell isn't repeatedly squashed by W_h and tanh, which is the constant error carousel.
